title: Messages & Roles: system, user, assistant, tool
summary: Chat models don't take a single string — they take an ordered list of messages, each tagged with a role: system (instructions), user (input), assistant (the model's replies, including tool-call requests), and tool (results your code feeds back). The whole list is re-sent every turn, and getting the roles and ordering right is what makes an agent loop actually work.
nestedConcepts: system vs user vs assistant roles

subtopics.title: A conversation is an ordered list of messages
subtopics.explanation: The chat API takes a list where each element is a dict with a role and content, in the exact order they occurred. The model reads that list top to bottom to decide the next reply. Everything an agent does is just appending the right message to this list, so it is the data structure at the heart of the whole loop.
subtopics.example:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise travel agent."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What's the capital of France?"},
]
# the model reads the list IN ORDER to produce the next message
reply = {"role": "assistant", "content": "Paris."}
messages.append(reply)

subtopics.title: system vs user vs assistant roles
subtopics.explanation: The system message sets durable instructions and persona and usually comes first; user messages carry human input; assistant messages are what the model itself produced, including any tool-call requests. Keeping these straight matters because the model treats system instructions as higher-priority context than user turns. Mislabeling a role can make the model ignore instructions or hallucinate that it already said something, breaking the loop's logic.
subtopics.example:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "Answer in one sentence."},   # rules
    {"role": "user", "content": "Explain gravity."},            # human
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Gravity pulls masses together."},  # model
]
# assistant turns are the model's OWN prior words -- never put user text here

subtopics.title: Tool results come back as a tool message with a call id
subtopics.explanation: When the model wants a tool, its assistant message contains a tool_call with an id; after your code runs the tool, you append a separate message with role 'tool' that carries the result and references that same tool_call_id. The id is how the model matches the result to the request it made. This request/response pairing is exactly how observations re-enter the conversation in an agent loop.

subtopics.title: The whole history is re-sent every turn
subtopics.explanation: LLMs are stateless: the model has no memory of prior calls, so on each turn you send the entire messages list again — that resend IS the memory. If you forget to append the assistant's last reply before the next user turn, the model loses the thread. This is also why history (and cost) grows every loop, tying directly back to the context-window budget.
subtopics.example:
def turn(messages, user_text, llm):
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    reply = llm(messages)                 # ENTIRE list is sent each call
    messages.append(reply)                # persist the model's own turn
    return reply

# every call re-sends system + user + assistant + tool history so far

subtopics.title: Ordering rules keep the transcript valid
subtopics.explanation: The list must read like a real dialogue: system typically first, roles alternate sensibly, and crucially every assistant tool_call must be followed by a matching tool message before the model runs again. Sending a tool result with no preceding tool_call, or leaving a tool_call unanswered, will error or confuse the model. Respecting this ordering is what keeps the agent loop from desyncing between request and observation.

foundations.overview: Every modern chat model exposes the same core interface: instead of a prompt string, you pass an ordered list of messages, each a small object with a role and content. Four roles carry the whole conversation. The system message holds durable instructions and persona; user messages are human input; assistant messages are the model's own outputs, which may include tool_call requests; and tool messages carry the results your code produced, linked back to a request by a tool_call_id. Because the model is stateless, you re-send this entire list on every turn — the list is the agent's memory — and there are ordering rules (system first, every tool_call answered by a tool message) that keep the transcript valid. Master this structure and the agent loop stops being magic and becomes list manipulation.
foundations.formalDefinition: A chat completion request is an ordered sequence of role-tagged messages M = [m1, m2, ...], where role in {system, user, assistant, tool}. Assistant messages may contain tool_calls, each with a unique id; a tool message must carry a tool_call_id matching a prior assistant tool_call. The model is stateless, so the full sequence is re-supplied on every call.
foundations.whyItMatters: The agent loop is nothing more than appending the correct message with the correct role to this list at the right time. Every capability — tool use, memory, RAG, multi-agent — is expressed by manipulating this structure, so getting roles and ordering right is the prerequisite for everything that follows.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a shared script for a play: system is the stage directions, user and assistant are two actors trading lines, and tool is a stagehand who runs offstage, does a task the assistant requested, and hands back a prop tagged with the exact request it answers. Each turn you hand the actors the whole script again because none of them remember the last scene.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Building the messages list for any chat call, appending assistant replies so context persists, feeding tool outputs back with the right tool_call_id in an agent loop, and validating transcript ordering before a request to avoid API errors.
foundations.performanceImpact: Because the entire list is re-sent every turn, input tokens (and cost/latency) grow with conversation length; well-structured, minimal messages keep an agent affordable, while duplicated or mislabeled turns waste budget and can degrade responses.
commonUseCases: Constructing the messages list for a chat completion
Appending assistant turns so history persists across calls
Feeding tool results back as tool messages in an agent loop
Validating role ordering before sending a request

commonMisconceptions.myth: The model remembers previous API calls.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Chat models are stateless. Any 'memory' is just the message list you resend each turn; drop a message and the model truly forgets it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can put a tool's result in a user message.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Tool results belong in a tool-role message with a matching tool_call_id. Mislabeling it as user text confuses the request/response pairing and can break tool use.
The model weights system instructions differently from user text and expects assistant turns to be its own prior words. Wrong roles change behavior and can cause it to ignore instructions.

interactiveExamples.title: Build a valid messages list turn by turn
interactiveExamples.explanation: Start with a system message, add a user turn, and persist the assistant's reply so the next turn has context. This is the minimal shape every chat call takes.

code.code:
messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise assistant."},
]

# user asks something
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "Capital of Japan?"})

# the model's reply is persisted as an assistant turn
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": "Tokyo."})

# a follow-up now has full context because we kept the history
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "And its population?"})

for m in messages:
    print(m["role"], "->", m["content"])
code.caption: Each turn is just an append; the growing list is the conversation's entire memory.
code.expectedOutput:
system -> You are a concise assistant.
user -> Capital of Japan?
assistant -> Tokyo.
user -> And its population?

interactiveExamples.title: Append a tool result with a matching call id
interactiveExamples.explanation: Simulate a full tool round-trip: the assistant requests a tool with an id, your code runs it, and you append a tool message referencing that same id so the model can match result to request.

code.code:
def get_weather(city):
    return f"{city}: 18C, light rain"

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris?"}]

# 1) model requests a tool call (id links request to result)
tool_call = {"id": "call_1", "name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": None, "tool_calls": [tool_call]})

# 2) your code executes the tool
result = get_weather(**tool_call["arguments"])

# 3) feed the observation back as a TOOL message with the same id
messages.append({
    "role": "tool",
    "tool_call_id": tool_call["id"],   # must match 'call_1'
    "content": result,
})

print(messages[-1]["role"], messages[-1]["tool_call_id"], "->", messages[-1]["content"])
code.caption: The tool_call_id is the thread that ties an observation back to the exact request that produced it.

codeLab.title: Implement a conversation manager
codeLab.instructions: Implement a small ConversationManager that (1) starts with a system message, (2) exposes add_user, add_assistant, and add_tool_result methods, and (3) validates that every tool message follows an assistant tool_call. add_tool_result must raise ValueError if the previous message is not an assistant message containing tool_calls. Fill in the methods so the test harness passes.
codeLab.testHarness:
cm = ConversationManager("You are a helper.")
cm.add_user("Weather in Paris?")
cm.add_assistant(tool_calls=[{"id": "c1", "name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}])
cm.add_tool_result("c1", "Paris: 18C")
assert cm.messages[0]["role"] == "system"
assert cm.messages[-1] == {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "c1", "content": "Paris: 18C"}

# invalid: tool result with no preceding tool_call
cm2 = ConversationManager("You are a helper.")
cm2.add_user("hi")
try:
    cm2.add_tool_result("x", "oops")
    raise AssertionError("should have raised")
except ValueError:
    pass
print("all tests passed")
hints: The system message goes in during __init__ so the list is never empty.
An assistant message may carry content, tool_calls, or both — only add the tool_calls key when it's provided.
In add_tool_result, inspect self.messages[-1]: it must have role 'assistant' and a 'tool_calls' key, otherwise raise ValueError.

checkpoints.prompt: Why must you re-send the entire messages list on every chat API call?
options: Because chat models are stateless and have no memory of prior calls
Because the system prompt changes each turn
checkpoints.explanation: The model keeps no server-side memory of your previous calls. The messages list you resend each turn IS the memory; drop a message and the model genuinely forgets it.

checkpoints.prompt: This code feeds a tool result back, but the loop breaks. What's the bug?
checkpoints.code:
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": None,
                 "tool_calls": [{"id": "call_1", "name": "get_weather",
                                 "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}]})
result = get_weather(city="Paris")
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": result})  # <-- here
options: The result is appended as a user message instead of a tool message with the matching tool_call_id
tool_calls must be a dict not a list
checkpoints.explanation: A tool's output must be a tool-role message carrying tool_call_id='call_1'. Labeling it as user text breaks the request/response pairing, so the model can't match the observation to its call.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print, given the model is stateless and we forget to persist its reply?
checkpoints.code:
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "Remember names."}]
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "My name is Sam."})
# (assistant replied 'Hi Sam' but we forgot to append it)
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "What's my name?"})
print([m["role"] for m in messages])
checkpoints.explanation: Only the messages we appended are present: system + two user turns. The missing assistant turn means that context is lost — a common cause of an agent 'forgetting' mid-conversation.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the tool message so the model can match the result to its request.
checkpoints.explanation: A tool message references the originating request via tool_call_id, which must match the id of the assistant's tool_call ('call_1').

theory.question: What are the four message roles in a chat API and what does each do?
theory.directAnswer: system carries durable instructions and persona; user carries human input; assistant carries the model's own outputs including tool-call requests; tool carries results your code produced, linked to a request by a tool_call_id.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A chat request is an ordered list of role-tagged messages, and the role tells the model what kind of content each message is and how to weight it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Roles let one flat list represent a structured dialogue — instructions, human turns, model turns, and tool results — so the model can reason about who said what.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: system usually leads and sets rules; user and assistant alternate as the human and the model speak; when the assistant requests a tool it emits a tool_call with an id, and after your code runs it you append a tool message with the matching tool_call_id so the model can pair result to request.

theory.whyImportant: The entire agent loop is expressed by appending the right role at the right time; mislabeling roles changes behavior and can break tool use.
theory.realWorldExample: A weather agent: system 'be concise', user 'weather in Paris?', assistant tool_call get_weather, tool message with the result, then assistant 'It's 18C and rainy.'

followUps.question: Can there be more than one system message?
followUps.answer: Usually there's one leading system message, though some providers allow additional ones. Keep durable instructions consolidated so they aren't diluted or contradicted.

followUps.question: What goes in an assistant message that requests a tool?
followUps.answer: Typically content is null or empty and a tool_calls list holds one or more calls, each with an id, a name, and arguments.

theory.question: Why is the full message history re-sent on every turn, and what are the implications?
theory.directAnswer: Chat models are stateless — they retain nothing between calls — so the messages list you resend each turn is the only memory. The implications are that you must persist every turn (including the model's own replies), and that input tokens, cost, and latency grow with conversation length.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Statelessness means each API call is independent; the model reconstructs all context solely from the messages you provide in that call.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It keeps the serving infrastructure simple and horizontally scalable — no per-user session state on the server — and puts context control in the client's hands.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You maintain the messages list client-side, append each user turn, assistant reply, and tool result, and pass the whole list every call. When it grows past the context window you trim or summarize it.

theory.whyImportant: It explains both the 'append the assistant reply' discipline and why long agent loops get expensive — directly linking messages to token-budget management.
theory.realWorldExample: An agent that loops eight times re-sends the accumulating history each time; forgetting to append an assistant turn makes it 'forget' what it just said, and never trimming makes cost balloon.

followUps.question: How do you keep resent history affordable?
followUps.answer: Trim or summarize old turns, avoid duplicating content, and use provider prompt-caching where available so unchanged prefixes aren't re-billed at full price.

followUps.question: Does the model ever store the conversation?
followUps.answer: Not as callable memory. Any persistence is on your side (or a provider convenience layer that still resends context under the hood).

scenario.question: Your agent works for one turn, then the provider returns a 400 error about an unanswered tool call. What's likely wrong and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: You appended an assistant message containing a tool_call but ran the model again before appending the matching tool message. Fix it by executing the tool and appending a tool-role message with the matching tool_call_id before the next model call.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A transcript-ordering violation: an assistant tool_call must be immediately answered by a tool message before the model is invoked again.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The provider validates that every tool_call has a corresponding tool result so the model isn't asked to continue with a dangling, unanswered request.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: In the loop, after the model returns tool_calls, iterate them, run each function, and append a tool message per call with its tool_call_id. Only then call the model again to get the next step.

scenario.whyImportant: This is one of the most common early agent bugs; understanding the ordering rule prevents desyncing the request/observation pairing.
scenario.realWorldExample: An agent emitted a get_weather call, but the code called the model again in the same iteration without appending the result — the second call errored until the tool message was inserted in between.

followUps.question: What if the model emits multiple tool_calls at once?
followUps.answer: Append one tool message per call id; all of them must be answered before the next model call, otherwise the same error occurs.

followUps.question: How would you catch this earlier?
followUps.answer: Run a validator that scans the list and asserts every assistant tool_call id has a following tool message before sending the request.

coding.question: Write a validator that returns True only if a messages list is well-formed: the first message is a system message and every tool message immediately follows an assistant message containing tool_calls.
coding.thoughtProcess: Two invariants to check. First, index 0 must be role 'system'. Second, for each tool message, the previous message must be an assistant with a 'tool_calls' key. I iterate with the index so I can look back one position, and I return False on the first violation.
lineByLine: Guard: an empty list or a non-system first message immediately fails.
Iterate with enumerate so each message knows its own index for a look-back.
Only tool messages need the ordering check; others pass through.
A tool message at index 0 is invalid because nothing precedes it.
The previous message must be an assistant with a tool_calls key, else the pairing is broken.
If no violation is found, the transcript is well-formed and we return True.
The __main__ block prints True then False for a valid and an invalid transcript.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) over the number of messages.

followUps.question: How would you also verify each tool_call id is answered?
followUps.answer: Collect all tool_call ids from assistant messages and all tool_call_ids from tool messages, then assert the sets match so no call is left dangling.

followUps.question: Would you enforce strict user/assistant alternation?
followUps.answer: Not strictly — tool messages and multi-tool turns break simple alternation. Validate the tool pairing and system-first rule rather than rigid alternation.

keyTakeaways: A chat request is an ordered list of role-tagged messages, not a single string.
The four roles are system (instructions), user (input), assistant (model output incl. tool calls), and tool (results your code returns).
Tool results go back as a tool message whose tool_call_id matches the assistant's original tool_call.
Models are stateless, so you re-send the whole list every turn — that resend is the agent's memory, and it drives cost/latency.
Ordering matters: system leads and every assistant tool_call must be answered by a tool message before the next model call.
